resources.string: The app can\'t install packages on this router
That needs the LuCI Software page (luci-app-package-manager, or luci-app-opkg before 24.10). Anything already installed still shows up and can be set up here.
It\'s installed, but its LuCI part (%1$s) is missing, and that\'s what lets the app configure it.
It\'s installed, but the router hasn\'t loaded it yet. The network needs a restart: a few seconds without connection.
The router will download %1$s and whatever it needs from the OpenWrt servers. It needs internet.
When it finishes, the network restarts: a few seconds without internet at home.
A firmware update removes installed packages; the app will let you know and you can install it again.
This phone will no longer be able to reach the router from outside home. It keeps working at home. You have to do this from home: the app removes it over the direct connection.
%1$s will no longer be able to reach the router from outside home.
Checks whether the router can be reached from the internet: the app tries over your mobile data, without leaving Wi-Fi. Uses a few KB.
The router can be reached from outside.
Can\'t check with this mobile data.
The router can\'t be reached from outside.
Only the app uses the tunnel, with its own WireGuard: it doesn\'t take the phone\'s VPN or touch others. Through the tunnel you can only reach the router\'s web page, not the rest of the network.
The router has no public address right now (neither IPv6 nor IPv4 without CGNAT): it can\'t be reached from outside.
It\'s reached over IPv6 (%1$s): the network you connect from must have IPv6 too.
WireGuard on UDP port %1$d · not up
From outside, the app will look for it at %1$s.
Without dynamic DNS, the app will use the last address it saw: if it changes while you\'re away, it won\'t find the router.

resources.string: Remote access needs it: without a fixed name, if your provider changes the router\'s address while you\'re away, the app won\'t find it.
For remote access: a name that always points to the router.
The router has no public IPv6 to publish right now.
Username (if the URL asks for one)
The router\'s IPv4 and IPv6 will be published: that way it can be reached from any network.
The router\'s IPv4 will be published.
The router\'s IPv6 will be published: with CGNAT, IPv4 can\'t be used to get in from outside.
This queue is on %1$s, but the internet connection is %2$s: this way it does nothing. Edit it to change it.
Write the speed without thousands separators (e.g. 1000).
Run a speed test with nobody else using the internet and enter a bit less (85–95 %): if you enter more than the connection gives, it won\'t help at all.
It\'s on, but the service isn\'t running.
No device can open ports on its own.
The router\'s internet address (%1$s) is private: there\'s another router in front or your provider uses CGNAT. So UPnP can\'t open ports to the internet over IPv4.
Each device can only open ports to itself. Best left on.
Encrypted tunnel so the app can reach the router when you\'re away from home.
A fixed name for the router, even if your ISP changes its address.
Keeps the connection from clogging up when someone downloads: video calls and games stay smooth.
Lets consoles and games open ports on their own (open NAT). Handy, but any device at home can open them.
Installing %1$s… It can take up to a minute.
The router installed the package but didn\'t load it. Restart it to finish.
There\'s already another active SQM queue on %1$s. Turn it off first.
That SQM queue no longer exists on the router: someone removed it from LuCI. Reload the screen.
UPnP has no configuration on the router. Reinstall it.
The router couldn\'t close that port. Reload the screen and try again.
There are no free addresses left in the router\'s remote access: remove a phone you no longer use.
The router\'s web server (uhttpd) only listens on %1$s. For remote access it has to listen on all IPv4 addresses (0.0.0.0) or on the LAN address.
The app is reaching the router through this phone\'s remote access right now: removing it would cut the connection. Remove it from home.
Enter at least one of the two speeds.
Below %1$s kbit/s the router would be left almost without a connection.
Free. On duckdns.org you sign in with your Google or GitHub account, pick a name and copy the token.
Free, with good IPv6 support. On dynv6.com you create a zone (e.g. myhome.dynv6.net) and copy its token.
Free and ad-free. On desec.io you register a dedyn.io name and create a token.
Your provider\'s update URL, with [DOMAIN], [USERNAME], [PASSWORD] and [IP] where they go. The app fills them in with the name, the username, the token and the router\'s address.
The token is missing (the key your provider gives you).
The token can\'t contain spaces or quotes.
The URL has to start with http:// or https://.
The URL has to include [IP], where the address goes.
The provider rejected the update: check the name and the token.
The router has no public address to publish (CGNAT without IPv6?).
The router is missing the HTTPS certificates (ca-bundle package).
The router couldn\'t connect to the provider: %1$s
Couldn\'t notify %1$s from the phone (no connection to its server). The router will publish its address in a few minutes, but an old address may stay published.
%1$s rejected the name or the token: check that the name is yours and the token was copied correctly.
The %1$s server failed. The router will try again in a few minutes.
dynv6 doesn\'t allow deleting the IPv6 address from here: if the name had an old one, remove it on dynv6.com.
Couldn\'t use mobile data. Turn it on (you can stay on Wi-Fi: the test only uses a few KB) and try again.
IPv6 (%1$s): the router didn\'t answer. It\'s almost always the ISP\'s modem dropping incoming IPv6 traffic: on its page, lower the IPv6 firewall level or put the router in its DMZ.
IPv6: your mobile data has no IPv6, so it couldn\'t be tested. It may be reachable from networks with IPv6.
IPv6: the router has no public IPv6. If your ISP provides IPv6, check the router\'s WAN6.
IPv4 (%1$s): not getting through. The router is behind another device (its WAN has %2$s): on that device, forward UDP port %3$d to the router or put it in its DMZ.
IPv4 (%1$s): the router didn\'t answer. Something in front of it may be dropping incoming traffic.
IPv4: your mobile data has no IPv4, so it couldn\'t be tested.
IPv4: the router is behind another device or a CGNAT (its WAN has %1$s), so it can\'t be reached over IPv4.
IPv4: the router has no public IPv4.
Without dynamic DNS, if your ISP changes the router\'s address, the app won\'t find it: set it up below.
Dynamic DNS still returns %1$s, which no longer belongs to the router (it updates every few minutes).
Dynamic DNS publishes %1$s, which doesn\'t get through: some programs try it first and fail to connect (WireGuard on Windows, for example). Better to publish only %2$s.
From outside, the dynamic DNS name doesn\'t return any address yet: the provider can take a few minutes.
Dynamic DNS didn\'t start on the router, so it was left as it was.
The router didn\'t remove dynamic DNS, so it was left as it was.
The router didn\'t remove remote access, so it was left as it was.
The router didn\'t bring up remote access (WireGuard), so it was left as it was.
The router stopped responding with the new SQM, so the change was undone.
UPnP didn\'t start on the router, so it was left as it was.
The router didn\'t apply the UPnP change, so it was left as it was.
